case_name: CASE OF MARKO TEŠIĆ v. SERBIA

assessment.Existence of an interference: The applicant, a defence lawyer, was fined 80,000 RSD for written submissions in which he criticized the presiding judge’s conduct during criminal proceedings, using strong language such as “truly outrageous!!!” and alleging procedural irregularities, including the judge’s alleged unlawful alteration of the court record (see paragraphs 10–11). The imposition of a fine for these expressions constitutes a clear interference with the applicant’s right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention, as it penalised his ability to voice professional criticism within the judicial process (see no. 28794/18).
assessment.Lawfulness of the interference: The interference had a basis in domestic law, namely Article 231 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which explicitly empowers courts to impose fines on participants in proceedings—including defence counsel—for insults or other forms of assault against the authority of the judiciary or other participants (see paragraph 16). As the domestic legal framework provided a clear and accessible basis for the sanction, the interference satisfied the requirement of lawfulness under Article 10 § 2 (see no. 31611/96).
assessment.Legitimate aims of the interference: The fine was imposed to protect the reputation of the judiciary and the authority of the court, as the presiding judge determined that the applicant’s statements belittled and insulted the panel (see paragraph 11). This aligns with the legitimate aim of ‘protecting the reputation or rights of others’ under Article 10 § 2, which includes safeguarding the dignity and authority of the judiciary (see no. 29045/95). Thus, the interference pursued a legitimate aim.
assessment.Necessary in a democratic society: While the interference pursued a legitimate aim, it was not ‘necessary in a democratic society’ under Article 10. The applicant’s submissions, though strongly worded, were directly tied to his professional duty to defend his client’s rights, addressing concrete procedural irregularities such as the omission of objections from the court record and alleged post-hearing alterations (see paragraphs 10 and 7–9). The European Court has consistently held that lawyers must enjoy a high degree of protection for expressions made in the course of judicial proceedings, even if critical or provocative, provided they do not overstep into gratuitous insults or baseless attacks (see no. 28794/18; see no. 31611/96). Here, the applicant’s language—while forceful—was contextualised by his role as defence counsel and the substance of his complaints. The domestic courts dismissed his appeal and constitutional complaint without adequately balancing his right to freedom of expression against the need to protect judicial authority, particularly given the lack of evidence that his remarks disrupted proceedings or undermined public trust in the judiciary. Moreover, the severity of the fine (RSD 80,000) and the absence of a less restrictive measure (e.g., a reprimand) render the interference disproportionate. The ECtHR has previously found violations in comparable cases where sanctions were imposed for professional criticism lacking a pressing social need (see no. 28794/18; see no. 29369/10).
